result.summary:
Novelty and prior-art review, cycle 1. The authors already concede that the pseudo-count mixture is not a new mechanism. They cite the closest works (Jeon 2026 Zenodo [29], Shahid 2026 arXiv:2606.20115, Rafe & Das 2026 arXiv:2605.05562, GHCP arXiv:2608.15500, TQA [22], Zhang et al. 2024 [28]) and include three of them as baselines. Web searches confirmed that arXiv 2605.05562, 2606.20115 and 2608.15500 exist and match how the paper describes them. Searches found nothing that directly anticipates a per-building onboarding benchmark for building loads. The head-to-head comparison in a new domain is therefore a legitimate applied contribution.

The remaining novelty claims are weaker than stated, and the paper's own results undercut one of them. In all six protocols, the fixed-pseudo-count donor-local mixture (the mechanism of prior work [29]) is more reliable than the authors' leave-one-building-out (LOBO) tuned variant. Yet the abstract and conclusion headline the tuned variant, and Section 2.3 lists "select the pseudo-count by LOBO rather than fixing it" as a point of difference. The "formalisation" of per-unit reliability (contribution 1) is essentially Lin et al.'s longitudinal and tail-coverage framework and has many 2026 counterparts. The negative finding on similarity priors rests on a single kNN design, while learned-grouping and localized calibration competitors are cited but not run.

Limitations of this review: arxiv.org and doi.org were not reachable from the review session, so I could check references only through search snippets. I could not independently confirm [29] or [14] (Hao et al., Appl Sci 2026).

issues.title: The authors' own results refute their main differentiator from the closest prior art [29]: the fixed pseudo-count beats the LOBO-tuned one everywhere
issues.evidence: Section 2.3 separates the paper from Jeon [29] by 'select the pseudo-count by leave-one-building-out rather than fixing it'. But HSC-CQR fixed-κ (κ = 168 h, which Section 4.3 itself calls 'a donor–local mixture with fixed pseudo-count as in [29]') is better than tuned HSC-CQR on MACD and under-covered share in every protocol. Main BDG2: 0.015 / 1.9% vs 0.018 / 3.4% (Table 5). UCI: 0.013 / 0.4% vs 0.014 / 0.6%. Leave-site-out: 0.016 / 1.7% vs 0.020 / 5.3%. BDG2→BDG2 without weather: 0.015 / 1.6% vs 0.017 / 2.9%. BDG2→UCI: 0.011 vs 0.013. UCI→BDG2: 0.019 / 4.3% vs 0.023 / 8.7% (supplementary T_gen tables). The paired CD test in Table 4 also goes against the tuned variant (BDG2 r_rb = -0.45, p < 0.001). Despite this, the abstract, highlights and conclusion report the tuned numbers (3.4%, 0.6%) as 'the most reliable strategy'.
issues.action: Remove LOBO tuning as a claimed advance over [29]. Either make the fixed or reliability-targeted pseudo-count the headline result, or state plainly that tuning on the interval score trades reliability for sharpness. Revise the abstract, highlights, the Section 2.3 positioning and the conclusion to match.
issues.experiment: Calibration-only rerun: select κ by LOBO on a reliability-aware objective (calibration-building MACD, or interval score subject to an under-coverage constraint). Report whether data-driven selection can match or beat κ = 168 across the six protocols. If it cannot, LOBO selection is not a contribution.

issues.title: Contribution 1 ('we formalise per-building reliability') and the problem framing are already established in prior work
issues.evidence: The paper's metrics (P10 of per-unit coverage, share of under-covered units, dispersion) mirror Lin, Trivedi & Sun's longitudinal coverage and least-covered-10% evaluation ([22, 44], which the paper cites). The point that pooled or marginal calibration hides unit-level under-coverage is the central finding of several 2026 preprints. Shahid, arXiv:2606.20115 reports violations at 40% of 20 sites. Rafe & Das, arXiv:2605.05562 report subgroup gaps of about 13 percentage points. 'When Is a Conformal Guarantee Fair? Auditing Silent Subgroup Under-Coverage in Alzheimer's Disease Longitudinal Prediction', arXiv:2608.04254 (2026), and arXiv:2605.14260 (2026) show that a pooled threshold hides group coverage distortion. Jeon [29] already frames the problem as cold-start conformal calibration for newly commissioned units.
issues.action: Reword contribution 1 as adopting and operationalising longitudinal per-unit reliability for building onboarding, not formalising it. Cite arXiv:2608.04254 and arXiv:2605.14260 as cross-domain evidence. Rest the novelty explicitly on the domain benchmark: the onboarding protocol, scale, transfer and stress tests.

issues.title: The claim that similarity adds nothing rests on one kNN design; learned-grouping and localized calibration competitors are cited but not run
issues.evidence: The conclusion and highlights state that 'similarity-weighted priors ... added nothing'. This is tested only with a kNN average over a hand-built 26-dimensional load-shape descriptor (Section 3.4 (ii)), plus Mondrian calibration by usage type. Clustered conformal prediction [47] and conditional calibration [46] are cited but not evaluated. Closely related 2026 methods borrow calibration information from units with similar score behaviour rather than similar inputs. 'Stochastic Grouping Conformal Prediction for Effective Subgroup Reliability' (arXiv:2610.11957; NeurIPS 2026 poster) learns such a grouping. RareCP (Heurich, Granz, Landgraf; arXiv:2605.08857, 2026) uses retrieval-weighted calibration quantiles combined with ACI. Prior work [29] also includes distance-weighted donors, so the negative result partly replicates prior work.
issues.action: Narrow the claim to 'kNN load-shape priors added nothing', or add competitors that group buildings by score behaviour. Discuss [29]'s distance-weighted donors as prior evidence.
issues.experiment: Calibration-only runs. (a) Clustered CP [47]: cluster calibration buildings on score-quantile embeddings and assign a new building by its early scores. (b) Conditional calibration [46] with the building descriptors as features. Report MACD and under-covered share on BDG2 and UCI.

issues.title: Energy-domain conformal prior art is missing, and the closest prior work is cited only as a code record
issues.evidence: Not cited: (1) Borrotti M., Energies 2024;17(17):4348, split conformal prediction for building heating and cooling loads. (2) 'Hierarchical Probabilistic Conformal Prediction' for distributed energy resources (arXiv:2411.12193). (3) TrustEnergy (arXiv:2601.14663), sequential CQR evaluated on more than 61,000 households; full author list not verified. Prior work [29] is a Zenodo software record. The repository's own audit (REVIEW/pre_review_audit_raw.json:126) notes that it accompanies a manuscript 'A two-network audit shows when conformal prediction intervals for solar irradiance forecasts remain valid at newly commissioned stations' (Scientific Reports, under review). The paper's positioning against [29] therefore depends on unreviewed grey literature.
issues.action: Add these works to Section 2.1. Cite the companion manuscript of [29], or state its status. Describe [29]'s mechanism precisely (donor–local mixture with fixed pseudo-count, distance-weighted donors, delayed-feedback ACI) so readers can judge the overlap.

issues.title: The 'HSC' name and Fig. 1 present elements that the paper shows are unnecessary, which suggests a new method
issues.evidence: The method is named 'hierarchical shrinkage conformal (HSC)' with three elements (Section 3.4, Fig. 1). Table 5 shows that stage matching and the kNN prior do nothing (MACD 0.017 / 0.017 / 0.017 vs 0.018). The configuration that works is a single pseudo-count mixture towards the pooled distribution, which is the Dirichlet-process or credibility form of [28, 52] and the mixture of [29]. On the absolute score, full HSC is beaten by Self-CP (0.029 vs 0.026).
issues.action: Present the recommended layer as plain pseudo-count (credibility) shrinkage of the pooled score distribution. Drop or soften the 'hierarchical' label, and move stage matching and the kNN prior into the ablation in Fig. 1 and Section 3.

issues.title: Some 2026 references could not be independently verified
issues.evidence: Targeted web searches found no trace of [14] (Hao, Yang & Ji, Appl Sci 2026;16:7984) or of [29]. Doi.org and arxiv.org were blocked from the review session. The repository's literature/verify_refs_new.py and references_verified_new.json claim Crossref and DataCite verification. [14] is used as the main domain evidence that split CP under-covers unseen buildings.
issues.action: Provide resolvable landing pages or DOIs for [14] and [29] in the response letter, and confirm that their content matches the paper's description.

result.summary: Methodology review, cycle 1. The core estimator in Eq. (5) is implemented as described. hsc_quantiles (calibration.py:173-210) uses only scores from earlier days (self_before is updated after the quantile is computed), adds the +1 to the denominator, and rounds grid quantiles up. The scale in Eq. (1) matches features.py:61-65. ACI, QShrink and the GHCP surrogate match Section 4.3, and the GHCP surrogate size of about 1344 is confirmed. I found no fatal error. Four problems need fixing before the claims hold. (1) The target-side sensitivity grid (results/sensitivity.csv) shows that the similarity-localised (kNN) prior pulls coverage down, yet leave-one-building-out tuning chose a finite K in every main run. The manuscript says this component 'added nothing', but the headline numbers come from the variant that includes it. (2) The TQA-B baseline sets its scaling parameter from all target buildings at once. This breaks the stated rule that target buildings are never used for any choice. (3) The 'two conformal limits' and Dirichlet-process statements are stronger than what the code computes. (4) Own scores are pooled across stages while the prior is stage-matched, and the explanation in Section 6.2 conflicts with the paper's own week-1 numbers. The claim that the method is 'most reliable' is also contradicted by the paper's own fixed-κ comparison in Table 4.

issues.title: The kNN-localised prior lowers coverage, but tuning selects it every time and the paper calls it neutral
issues.evidence: results/sensitivity.csv (target buildings, mean over seeds). BDG2 absolute score at κ=∞: mean coverage 0.841 with K=10 versus 0.881 with K=all; under-covered share 45.9% versus 29.0%. UCI absolute score at κ=∞: 0.857 versus 0.903. At the selected κ=336 (absolute score): under-covered 16.1% with K=10 versus 10.1% with K=all. Coverage is lower with kNN at every κ and on both datasets, including the CQR score (BDG2 κ=168: 0.892 versus 0.895). Table 5: 'HSC -shrink' (kNN prior) leaves 45.8% under-covered versus 29.0% for SCP-stage; HSC 9.2% versus HSC -kNN 5.3%. The first-week coverage of HSC-CQR (0.885) is below CQR (0.892), whereas HSC-CQR simple reaches 0.895. This contradicts Section 5.3, which says every strategy is 'only as reliable as its population calibration'. run_info.json: tuning chose K∈{10,25,50,100}, never 'all', for HSC and HSC-CQR in all 10 main runs at α=0.1. Sections 5.4, 5.7 and 6.2 say the prior 'produced no measurable gain' and that 'K has little influence'. Likely mechanism: an unweighted average over the K nearest neighbours in standardised space pulls atypical, volatile buildings towards more typical neighbours, which gives them priors that are too narrow. The descriptor has 24 profile dimensions and only one load-level dimension. Tuning probably fails to catch this because leave-one-building-out keeps buildings from the same site in the same period, so their errors are correlated.
issues.action: Report the kNN prior as harmful for the absolute score and as reducing first-week coverage, not as neutral. Base the abstract, highlights and conclusion on the recommended simple variant, or show both variants. Explain the bias, for example by plotting each target's prior quantile against its realised own quantile, split by descriptor volatility.
issues.experiment: Re-run tuning with calibration buildings held out by site (or by site and time) on BDG2, and check whether finite K is still selected. Report coverage at κ=∞ for kNN, distance-weighted kNN and K=all, all from the stored scores.

issues.title: The TQA-B baseline uses target-set information that is not available at forecast time
issues.evidence: calibration.py:325-326: `gmax = g.max()` is taken over all target buildings at that stage, and λ=min(1,(α−0.01)/gmax) is then applied to every target. So each building's radius depends on the other target buildings in the same stage. This contradicts pipeline.py:12 and Section 3.4 ('Target buildings are never used for any choice'). Section 4.3 describes λ as 'chosen per stage' without saying that it is computed across targets.
issues.action: Compute λ from calibration-building ranks only, or clip each building's adjustment individually. Re-run TQA-B-CQR and update Tables 2-4, 6 and 7.
issues.experiment: Recompute TQA-B-CQR for all runs. This needs no retraining: only the calibration step is repeated.

issues.title: The headline 'most reliable strategy' is the tuned full variant, but a fixed κ is more reliable on the paper's own tests
issues.evidence: Table 4, BDG2: HSC-CQR versus fixed-κ on coverage deviation gives mean difference +0.0026, CI [+0.0015, +0.0036], r_rb=−0.45, p<0.001, i.e. the fixed-κ variant is better. Table 5: fixed-κ has MACD 0.015 and 1.9% under-covered, versus 0.018 and 3.4% for the tuned variant. The objective used for tuning (interval score) picked κ=336 in all BDG2 runs, while MACD is lowest at κ=96-168 (Fig. 9). Abstract and conclusion: 'Score-distribution shrinkage was the most reliable strategy… 3.4%'.
issues.action: State in the abstract and conclusion that the tuned κ trades reliability for sharpness, and that one week of hourly scores is the more reliable setting. Alternatively, pre-specify a tuning objective that targets coverage (for example interval score plus a penalty on under-coverage) and report it as a sensitivity analysis.
issues.experiment: Optional: tuning by coverage deviation on calibration buildings, using the stored scores.

issues.title: The 'two conformal limits' and Dirichlet-process readings are overstated
issues.evidence: calibration.py:201-204: for κ=∞ the code takes the quantile of a building-weighted average of K empirical CDFs, at level ⌈(1−α)(N+1)⌉/N with N the number of hourly scores. That is neither split conformal on pooled scores nor building-level hierarchical conformal (where the exchangeable unit is the building, so the correction should involve K rather than N≈K·24·bin size). The test point added at +∞ in Eq. (5) also means the expression is not a Dirichlet-process posterior mean. In addition, calibration scores come from 2016 and targets from 2017, so even the two limits lack exchangeability.
issues.action: Rephrase. The limits reproduce the form of split-conformal and self-only calibration but carry no guarantee under this protocol. Eq. (5) is a posterior mean with an added conservative point mass, not the posterior itself. Either cite building-level corrections (Dunn et al., Lee et al.) or state that the hour-level correction is negligible and has no formal meaning here.

issues.title: The prior is stage-matched but the building's own scores are pooled across stages, and the explanation in Section 6.2 conflicts with the data
issues.evidence: hsc_quantiles adds own scores from every earlier stage into one pool (self_before, calibration.py:193,209), while the prior comes only from bin B(h). Section 6.2 says stage matching was unnecessary because 'errors at different stages are already on a comparable scale'. Yet Table 2 shows SCP week-1 coverage of 0.863 versus 0.888 for SCP-stage, and Table 5 / T_ablation shows HSC -stage week-1 coverage of 0.863 versus 0.880 for HSC. Stage effects are therefore present for the absolute score.
issues.action: Limit the claim that stage matching is unnecessary to the CQR score. Acknowledge the inconsistency in how stages are treated within Eq. (5), or test recency- or stage-weighted own scores.

issues.title: Nothing prevents inverted intervals when the CQR radius is negative
issues.evidence: The grid extends to −10 s, and band() at pipeline.py:259 applies q without a lower bound. For 16.6% of BDG2 building-seeds, the HSC-CQR width is below the QR-LGBM width, so the mean q is negative (Self-CQR: 24.3%). metrics.py:25 counts hi−lo even when it is negative, which lowers the interval score and makes it improper for inverted intervals.
issues.action: Report how many hours have lo>hi, and either clip the width at zero or replace inverted intervals by their midpoint for every method.

issues.title: Smaller inconsistencies between the manuscript and the code
issues.evidence: (a) Section 3.2 says training history length is drawn 'uniformly from {1,…,28}', but pipeline.py:86 truncates it to t−p0 near the start of the period. (b) For UCI, K=100 is at least the size of the calibration pool, so in sensitivity.csv the K=100 and K=all rows are identical; selections of 'K=100' (for example UCI s3) are really K=all. (c) The UCI LightGBM mean training time of 298 s in Table 8 is driven by one outlier (s1: 1316 s, against roughly 26-52 s for the other seeds); report the median.
issues.action: Correct the text. Cap the K grid at the pool size, or label such selections as K=all. Report median computation times.

result.summary:
I reviewed this as the experimental-design reviewer, cycle 1. The protocol itself is sound. Buildings and periods are disjoint, the main hyper-parameters are tuned only by leave-one-building-out (LOBO) on calibration buildings, all tuning tables are stored in run_info.json, and competitors share the forecaster, the scores and the grid. The problem is that several headline claims are not what the executed experiments support.

1. The cold-start premise ("reliable from the first days") does not hold in week 1. I recomputed per-building metrics from results/raw_results.csv.gz using the coverage_early column (stages h ≤ 7, metrics.py:15). In week 1, HSC-CQR leaves more buildings under-covered than pooled CQR.
2. The untuned fixed-κ variant (κ = 168 h) beats the LOBO-tuned headline method on reliability in every one of the 15 settings that were run. It is hidden from Tables 6 and 7.
3. The method in the headline is not the one the pre-registration named as primary.
4. The α-sensitivity runs leave out every CQR-based method.
5. The robustness narrative picks favourable comparisons.

The fixes need mostly reporting, re-tabulation and a few cheap calibration-only re-runs. The trained models are cached, so no retraining is needed.

issues.title: No per-building reliability gain in the first week, which the paper says is its target
issues.evidence: I recomputed per-building week-1 metrics from raw_results.csv.gz (exp=main, α=0.1; seed means; coverage_early = h ≤ 7, metrics.py:15). Share of buildings under-covered in week 1, BDG2: HSC-CQR 24.5%, CQR 23.8%, GHCP-CQR 22.0%, TQA-B-CQR 22.4%, QShrink-CQR 21.5%, fixed-κ 19.8%. UCI: HSC-CQR 17.5%, CQR 16.0%, GHCP 13.1%, QShrink 14.5%. Week-1 MACD, BDG2: HSC-CQR 0.051 vs CQR 0.061, so only a small gain. Table 2 also shows mean week-1 coverage of 0.885 for HSC-CQR against 0.892 for CQR. All of the reported gain comes from weeks 2–8 (late-window MACD 0.020 vs 0.039). Yet the abstract, Section 3.1 ('from the first days after metering starts') and the pre-registered hypothesis H0 ('most severely in the first week') present cold start as the target.
issues.action: Add a table of per-building metrics by onboarding stage: week 1, week 2 and weeks 3–8. Give MACD, under-covered share and P10 coverage for all CQR-family methods, with paired tests, plus the sampling-noise floor for 168 hourly observations. Rewrite the abstract, highlights and conclusion to say that the benefit appears from about week 2 onward, and that in week 1 no strategy beats pooled calibration.
issues.experiment: None; this is a re-analysis of existing raw results.

issues.title: The untuned fixed-κ variant beats the LOBO-tuned headline method everywhere, and is omitted from the robustness and generalisation tables
issues.evidence: The LOBO objective is almost flat. In run_info.json (lso_BDG2_f0, K = 25), the objective is 0.52078 at κ = 336 and 0.52160 at κ = 168. Even so, it picks κ = 336 in 9 of 10 BDG2 runs (hsc_cqr entries). HSC-CQR fixed-κ (κ = 168) was run in all lso, xds and robust experiments, and it gives lower MACD and a lower under-covered share than tuned HSC-CQR in every setting. Examples: leave-site-out 0.016 / 1.7% vs 0.020 / 5.3%; UCI→BDG2 0.019 / 4.3% vs 0.023 / 8.7%; 10% calibration pool 0.016 / 2.2% vs 0.020 / 7.9%; level shift +40% 0.017 / 2.8% vs 0.021 / 6.5%. Tables 6 and 7 leave it out. The abstract nevertheless calls the LOBO-selected HSC-CQR 'the most reliable strategy'.
issues.action: Report fixed-κ in Tables 6 and 7 and in Fig. 7 and Fig. 8. Either pre-specify κ, or tune with an objective that matches the stated target, for example interval score with a per-building under-coverage penalty or a coverage-deviation term. Apply the same choice to QShrink, so that a fixed-κ HSC is not compared against a tuned QShrink. Stop presenting LOBO selection as a contribution unless it beats the fixed choice.
issues.experiment: Run QShrink-CQR with fixed λ = 168 and, optionally, a reliability-aware LOBO objective for both HSC-CQR and QShrink-CQR. This is calibration only and reuses the cached models.

issues.title: The 'pre-registered' label is overstated: the primary method changed and the design changed after an early look at target results
issues.evidence: PREREGISTRATION.md names HSC on absolute scores as the primary method and lists 'HSC on CQR scores' only as a variant under Baselines. CHANGELOG (2026-11-16) instead says 'Pre-registered primary comparison remains HSC-CQR'. The pre-registered primary method HSC loses to Self-CP (MACD 0.029 vs 0.026) and has a worse interval score than CQR (0.642 vs 0.564, Table 2). REVIEW_HISTORY records a 'first full-run look (seed 0 BDG2)' before several changes were made: GHCP, TQA-B, QShrink, the simple variant and fixed-κ were added, the ACI grid was changed, and ablations were removed. After those changes, all results were recomputed. The abstract still says 'under a pre-registered ... protocol'.
issues.action: Add a table of deviations from the pre-registration (what changed, when, whether it was before or after target results were seen, and why). Report the pre-registered primary comparison, HSC vs the baselines, prominently. Either qualify 'pre-registered' in the abstract or remove it.
issues.experiment: None

issues.title: The α-sensitivity runs do not test the headline method or any of its real competitors
issues.evidence: In raw_results, the runs at α = 0.05 and α = 0.2 contain only ACI, HSC, HSC simple, MLP-Gauss, Mondrian-usage, Naive+SCP, Raw-SCP, SCP, SCP-stage and Self-CP. HSC-CQR, QShrink-CQR, Self-CQR, ACI-CQR, TQA-B-CQR, GHCP-CQR and CQR are all missing. At 95% on BDG2, Self-CP beats HSC (MACD 0.017 vs 0.019, T_alpha0.05_BDG2). Section 5.7 restricts its claim to 'absolute-score strategies', but the conclusions are written about HSC-CQR.
issues.action: Run the CQR-family comparison at α = 0.05 and α = 0.2, at least for 3 seeds, and report it in Tables S3–S6. Otherwise, explicitly limit all claims to the 90% level.
issues.experiment: E7 for the CQR-family methods. The quantile models at α/2 and 1 − α/2 must be retrained for each α.

issues.title: The robustness narrative picks favourable comparisons, and the stress-test design favours methods that use the building's own scores
issues.evidence: Table 6: under 15% meter noise, Self-CQR reaches 0.010 / 0%, better than HSC-CQR at 0.018 / 2%; the text mentions only HSC-CQR's 1.7%. With a 10% calibration pool, HSC-CQR leaves 7.9% under-covered, more than QShrink (5.9%) and Self-CQR (7.0%). With 20% missing data, QShrink is at 3.4% vs 4.0% for HSC-CQR. In src/experiments.py:151-158, the noise is i.i.d. homoscedastic Gaussian with sd equal to the noise level times the window mean, and it is added to the evaluation truth as well. That is an exchangeable noise component which structurally rewards any method that uses own scores. The stress tests use 3 seeds, and statistics.csv contains no paired tests for the robust experiments.
issues.action: Rewrite Section 5.5 to report the best method under each condition. Add a realistic noise model, such as heteroscedastic or autocorrelated multiplicative noise, or noise applied to history only. Add paired per-building tests for the stress tests.
issues.experiment: Optional: one extra noise variant and the paired tests on the existing robust results.

issues.title: Competitors get unequal tuning budgets
issues.evidence: HSC-CQR searches 45 (κ, K) configurations. QShrink searches 9 values of λ and ACI-CQR 8 values of γ. TQA-B-CQR has a fixed decay of 0.8 per day and a constrained λ, and GHCP-CQR has a fixed surrogate group size of about 1344 and a fixed new-building weight. Neither is tuned. Self-CQR uses all past own scores, with no tuned window or recency weighting.
issues.action: Tune TQA-B's decay and GHCP's new-group weight (or surrogate size) by the same LOBO procedure. Add a Self-CQR with a tuned rolling window. State the tuning budget of every method in a table.
issues.experiment: LOBO grids for TQA-B, GHCP and Self-CQR. Calibration only.

issues.title: Wilcoxon p-values ignore site clustering, and mean differences are dominated by capped radii
issues.evidence: statistics.csv reports leave-site-out HSC-CQR vs QShrink-CQR abs_dev with p_holm = 1.2e-15. Those buildings come from only 10 sites in 5 folds, yet each building is treated as independent. In Table 4, the UCI ACI-CQR interval-score mean difference is −1.91 with CI [−4.60, −0.15]. That number is driven by the conservative 500·s radius cap, not by typical behaviour.
issues.action: Use cluster-aware tests (site-level permutation or a mixed model) for BDG2. In Table 4, report median or trimmed-mean differences alongside the means.
issues.experiment: None

result.summary: Statistical review, cycle 1. I spot-checked numbers against results/statistics.csv and raw_results.csv.gz and they match the text. Examples: BDG2 HSC-CQR vs CQR coverage-deviation (CD) mean difference -0.0204 with r_rb 0.86; n = 713 unique target buildings out of 1265 building x seed units. The main claim holds, and holds at site level too: HSC-CQR beats CQR at all 10 BDG2 sites (site-level Wilcoxon p = 0.002). The weaknesses are in inference and reporting, not arithmetic. (1) The Wilcoxon tests treat buildings as independent, but the confidence intervals use a site-cluster bootstrap, and only 10 sites of very unequal size exist; for small effects the two disagree. (2) Claims of robustness and generalisation are not backed by the paired tests the pipeline already computes, and in several stress conditions those tests contradict them. (3) The ablation tests are left out and the ablation text misdescribes them. The headline comparator (full HSC-CQR) is significantly worse on CD than both the simple and the fixed-kappa variants the paper recommends. (4) Holm families are defined inconsistently. (5) Mean interval-score differences are dominated by ACI blow-ups. (6) The headline under-covered share has no interval and no test. All of this can be fixed by re-analysing the existing results; no new experiments are needed.

issues.title: Building-level Wilcoxon p-values ignore site clustering; the 10-cluster bootstrap is fragile
issues.evidence: The Methods (Sec. 4.4) say buildings at a site share weather and operation, which is why the confidence intervals come from a site-cluster bootstrap. The Wilcoxon test in src/statistics/analysis.py:paired_tests still treats the 713 buildings as independent. The two disagree. HSC-CQR vs HSC-CQR -kNN on CD: p_holm = 2.8e-4, but the cluster CI is [-0.0003, +0.0012]. HSC-CQR vs simple: p_holm = 7e-5, CI [-0.0003, +0.0014]. When I recomputed the -kNN and simple comparisons on site-mean differences, the Wilcoxon p was 0.85 for both. The clusters are also very unequal: Rat has 218 of 713 buildings and Moose has 5. A percentile bootstrap over G = 10 such clusters is known to under-cover. Failure rates also differ by site: HSC-CQR leaves 13.3% under-covered at Wolf and 7.9% at Robin, against 3.4% overall. This is not reported.
issues.action: Add a cluster-aware test as the primary inference, for example a site-level permutation or sign-flip test, a wild cluster bootstrap, or a mixed model with a site random effect. Report it next to the building-level Wilcoxon, and state that the building-level p-values are conditional on independence. Report per-site under-coverage in a supplementary table.
issues.experiment: Re-analysis only (existing raw_results).

issues.title: Robustness and generalisation claims are not backed by, and sometimes contradict, the computed paired tests
issues.evidence: Sec. 5.5/5.6 and the Conclusion say HSC-CQR 'remained beneficial' and is 'the most reliable', and Sec. 5.5 orders HSC-CQR ahead of QShrink-CQR (4.2% vs 5.9% under level -40%). statistics.csv shows the following. vs Self-CQR on CD: leave-site-out p_holm = 0.96, UCI->BDG2 p = 0.18, missing40 p = 0.78, shift+40 p = 1.0, weak forecaster p = 0.50, calpool10 p = 0.013 (r = 0.12). Under noise15, Self-CQR is significantly better (r_rb = -0.66, p = 3.8e-41). vs QShrink-CQR on CD: under calpool10, QShrink is significantly better (r = -0.23, p = 1.4e-5); differences are not significant under shift-40 (p = 0.11), shift+40 (p = 1.0), noise5 (p = 0.13) and calpool50 (p = 0.47). Table 6 and Table 7 report no tests at all.
issues.action: Add a supplementary test table for every stress and transfer condition (CD and IS, with cluster-aware p-values and effect sizes). Revise Sec. 5.5/5.6, the Conclusion and the Highlights: HSC-CQR's advantage over self-only and quantile shrinkage is clear in the random-building protocol, but under stress and transfer it is often not significant, and in some conditions it is reversed.

issues.title: Ablation tests are omitted and misdescribed; the headline comparator is not the recommended configuration
issues.evidence: Sec. 5.4 says removing the kNN prior or stage matching 'changes the MACD by less than its seed-to-seed standard deviation' and that they 'add nothing'. The computed building-level tests show the full HSC-CQR is significantly worse on CD than -stage (r = -0.18, p_holm = 1.4e-4), -kNN (r = -0.16, p = 2.8e-4) and simple (r = -0.19, p = 7e-5). Fixed-kappa beats the tuned HSC-CQR on under-coverage in 5 of 5 BDG2 seeds (1.9% vs 3.4%; CD r = -0.45). Even so, Table 4 and the abstract use the full HSC-CQR, while the paper recommends a one-parameter layer with kappa of 'one to two weeks'. Comparing seed s.d. values is not an equivalence test.
issues.action: Report the ablation tests with cluster-aware p-values. Replace the 'less than s.d.' argument with an equivalence test (TOST) against a pre-stated margin, for example the 0.0066 MACD noise floor. Use the recommended configuration (HSC-CQR simple, or fixed kappa) as the primary comparator in Table 4 and the abstract, or justify the current choice; the HSC-CQR simple vs baseline tests already exist in statistics.csv.

issues.title: Holm family definition in Table 4 does not match the code; no correction across conditions
issues.evidence: The Table 4 caption says 'Holm-adjusted within dataset and metric'. analysis.py:139-142 applies Holm separately within each paired_tests() call. The fixed-kappa rows come from the 5-test ablation family, so their adjusted p-values are not comparable with the 15-baseline family in the same table. statistics.csv has 570 tests, and the 10 robustness conditions, 4 transfer settings and 3 alpha levels are each corrected separately.
issues.action: Define the families explicitly in Sec. 4.4 and fix the caption. Either adjust within a declared confirmatory family (the main CQR-family comparisons) and label all other tests exploratory, or apply Holm or BY correction across conditions.

issues.title: Mean interval-score differences are dominated by ACI blow-ups; effect estimate and test disagree
issues.evidence: Table 4 reports ACI-CQR IS mean differences of -1.914 on UCI (CI [-4.60, -0.15]) and -0.172 on BDG2 (CI [-0.505, -0.002]); statistics.csv has UCI->BDG2 at -3.67. These come from the radius cap at 500*s when alpha_h <= 0, while the medians are about -0.001. MLP-QR on UCI IS: CI [-0.0119, +0.0072] includes 0, yet p < 0.001 and HSC-CQR is better for 77% of buildings. QShrink on BDG2 IS: CI [-0.0098, -0.0000] excludes 0, yet p = 0.688 and the text calls them 'statistically indistinguishable'.
issues.action: Report the median difference (already computed) or the Hodges-Lehmann estimate, with a CI that matches the signed-rank test. Show how often ACI's radius hits the cap. Keep the mean only as a secondary statistic.

issues.title: The headline under-covered share has no interval and no test
issues.evidence: The abstract headline (3.4% / 0.6% vs 18.7% / 9.5%) is reported only as mean +/- s.d. over seeds, computed on overlapping target sets. The UCI figure of 0.6% is 3 of 475 units (MT_140, MT_066, MT_093), with zero in 3 of 5 seeds and s.d. 0.9 > mean. The tests cover only the continuous CD and IS.
issues.action: Add a paired inference for the under-covered indicator: a cluster-bootstrap CI for the difference in shares, or McNemar on per-building indicators. Give interval estimates next to the headline numbers.

issues.title: Error-analysis tests pseudo-replicate and lack uncertainty
issues.evidence: Sec. 5.8 runs Mann-Whitney on building x seed units: 43 units covering 39 distinct buildings on BDG2, and 3 units on UCI. The Spearman correlations (-0.65 / -0.36 / -0.96) have no CI, and building duplicates across seeds are not handled.

result.summary:
Robustness and generalisation review, cycle 1. The method was tested on BDG2 and UCI with leave-site-out, cross-dataset transfer and six stress conditions. The comparison is wide, and the numbers I checked match results/raw_results.csv.gz. Several stress tests are built in ways that favour own-score methods, or are too mild to back the robustness claims in the Abstract, Section 5.5 and the Conclusion.

(1) The "newly metered" claim fails in week 1. I recomputed first-week (h<=7) per-building under-coverage from raw_results. HSC-CQR leaves 24.5% of BDG2 buildings under-covered against 23.8% for CQR, and 17.5% against 16.0% on UCI. The same pattern holds in every protocol: LSO 27.7 vs 26.4, UCI->BDG2 37.9 vs 37.3. All gains come after the first week.

(2) The "weak forecaster" is barely weaker. Its CV(RMSE) is 0.137/0.145/0.140 against 0.134/0.139/0.131 for the main models (run_info.json).

(3) The noise test adds i.i.d. homoscedastic noise to the evaluation truth. This favours own-score calibration by construction: Self-CQR is best there (0.010 / 0.1%).

(4) Missing data are hour-wise MCAR, not outage blocks. The level shift is one step at day 28, which the 7-day scale normalisation largely absorbs.

(5) The full HSC-CQR is not the most reliable variant under leave-site-out or with a small calibration pool, yet the headline numbers use it.

(6) Robustness was run on BDG2 only, with 3 seeds and no dispersion or paired tests. There are no seasonal, holiday, weather-forecast-error or longer-horizon tests.

None of this is fatal, but the claims need targeted new experiments or must be narrowed.

issues.title: No per-building reliability gain in the first onboarding week, the regime the paper's title and framing target
issues.evidence: Recomputed from results/raw_results.csv.gz (coverage_early, h<=7; main protocol, alpha=0.1), share of buildings with first-week coverage <0.85. BDG2: HSC-CQR 24.5%, CQR 23.8%, QShrink 21.5%, fixed-κ 19.8%, Self-CQR 33.7%. UCI: HSC-CQR 17.5%, CQR 16.0%. Also LSO 27.7 vs 26.4, UCI->BDG2 37.9 vs 37.3, BDG2->UCI 15.4 vs 14.7. Mean week-1 coverage is lower for HSC-CQR (0.885 vs 0.892, Table 2). The manuscript only says 'every strategy can only be as reliable as its population calibration' (Sec 5.3), but the Highlights and Abstract still claim reliability 'from the first days after a building is metered'.
issues.action: Report per-building week-1 under-coverage (and P10) for all methods in Tables 2, 3 and 7. Narrow the claims: the gain appears from week 2 onwards. Put a sampling-noise reference next to it: with n=168 and alpha=0.1 the iid floor is about 1.5%, higher with autocorrelation. Report coverage stratified by onboarding stage (days 1-3, 4-7, 8-14).
issues.experiment: Evaluate the week-1 per-building coverage distribution for all CQR-score methods. Optionally test a conservative cold-start rule, e.g. inflating the prior quantile when n_own is small, or using the building's stage-1 descriptor to pick a wider prior, to see whether week 1 can be fixed.

issues.title: The 'weak forecaster' stress test does not produce a weak forecaster
issues.evidence: results/run_info.json, point CV(RMSE). Weak model: 0.137 (s0), 0.145 (s1), 0.140 (s2). Main/full model on the same seeds: 0.134, 0.139, 0.131, i.e. only 2-7% worse; seasonal naive is 0.19-0.21. Sec 5.5 and the Conclusion nevertheless claim the method 'remained beneficial ... [with] a weak forecaster'. Naive+SCP exists, but HSC was never applied to a genuinely poor forecaster.
issues.action: Rename the condition ('reduced training pool') or replace it with genuinely degraded forecasters. Report their point accuracy in Table 6.
issues.experiment: Apply HSC-CQR / QShrink / Self-CQR / CQR on top of (a) the seasonal-naive point forecast with abs scores (HSC on Naive), (b) a LightGBM without lag and profile features, and (c) a model trained on 1-2% of buildings. Report MACD, under-coverage share, week-1 under-coverage and IS.

issues.title: Meter-noise test is built to favour own-score methods and does not model meter error
issues.evidence: src/experiments.py:151-159 adds N(0, level*mean(window)) i.i.d. homoscedastic noise to the whole target window, including the truth used for evaluation. The test therefore inflates irreducible, exchangeable noise that the building's own scores capture perfectly, so Self-CQR wins (noise15: MACD 0.010, under 0.1%, vs HSC-CQR 0.018 / 1.7%; T_robustness.md). SCP-stage reaching 100% under-coverage is an artefact of comparing clean calibration with an artificially noisier truth. The text presents this as HSC robustness.
issues.action: Reframe this condition as 'added irreducible noise', state that Self-CQR is best, and add realistic sensor-error scenarios.
issues.experiment: (a) Noise on inputs/history only, with truth kept clean. (b) Heavy-tailed or spike errors (e.g. 1% of hours x5 or zero readings, meter resets). (c) Heteroscedastic, load-proportional noise. (d) A calibration-population contamination test: noisy calibration buildings with clean targets.

issues.title: Missing-data and level-shift scenarios are the easiest variants
issues.evidence: perturb_missing (experiments.py:162) drops hours MCAR, while real outages are contiguous blocks; the paper's own quality rule interpolates gaps <=6 h. perturb_shift (experiments.py:173) applies one multiplicative step at day 28 to every building. Because the scale s uses the last 7 days (Eq. 1), normalised scores recover within a week, so the test is mild. As expected, week-1 metrics are identical to the clean run (shift+40 and shift-40 week-1 under-coverage both 26.0% for HSC-CQR). The remaining HSC failures are linked to regime change (Sec 5.8: level-change median 0.197 vs 0.053), yet no shape, volatility or early-shift scenario was run.
issues.action: Add realistic disruption scenarios and report post-change coverage separately (days after the change).
issues.experiment: (a) Block outages of 1-7 days, including at onboarding start. (b) Shifts at day 3, 7 and 49. (c) Schedule or shape changes (e.g. weekend/weekday swap, a shifted occupancy profile) and a doubling of volatility at fixed mean. (d) Gradual drift. (e) A 6-12-month horizon to check whether stale own scores hurt after a regime change, with a recency-weighted variant as an ablation.

issues.title: Headline variant (full HSC-CQR) is not the most reliable under transfer and small pools; claims of superiority are not supported there
issues.evidence: Table 7 and T_gen_leave-site-out.md, LSO under-coverage: HSC-CQR 5.3% vs fixed-κ 1.7%, simple 3.5%, QShrink 4.2%; MACD fixed-κ 0.016 vs HSC-CQR 0.020. Per fold (my recomputation): fold 1 (Hog, Moose) HSC-CQR 6.4% vs ACI-CQR 4.3%; fold 0 (Rat, 248 buildings) Self-CQR 2.0% vs HSC-CQR 6.5%. Cal pool 10% (Table 6): HSC-CQR 7.9% vs QShrink 5.9% and simple 6.2%, with LOBO κ dropping to 24-48 h (run_info). UCI->BDG2: QShrink and Self-CQR are statistically comparable to HSC-CQR. Under shift, the LOBO-tuned κ is the weak link.
issues.action: Report per-fold LSO results with paired tests (HSC variants vs QShrink and Self-CQR). State that the tuned full variant is not uniformly best. Consider making the fixed or simple variant the primary method, and justify κ-selection robustness.
issues.experiment: Paired per-building Wilcoxon tests and site-cluster CIs for the LSO, cross-dataset and stress conditions. Calibration-pool sizes of 5, 10, 20 and 40 buildings with κ fixed vs LOBO-tuned, to show whether tuning on tiny pools is harmful.

issues.title: Robustness evidence is BDG2-only, 3 seeds, with no dispersion or significance
issues.evidence: Table 6 / T_robustness.md give seed means only. Differences between HSC-CQR, HSC-CQR simple and QShrink-CQR are 1-2 points (e.g. missing20: 4.0% vs 3.3% vs 3.4%) without s.d. or tests. No UCI robustness runs exist (experiments.py plan(): robust/weak jobs for BDG2 only).
issues.action: Add s.d. over seeds and paired tests to Table 6, and avoid ranking claims within noise.
issues.experiment: Repeat the stress suite on UCI (and on the LSO folds) with 5 seeds.

issues.title: Untested deployment shifts: seasonality and holidays, weather-forecast errors, calibration-target period gap
issues.evidence: Onboarding dates are uniform over the target year (pipeline.py:121-132), and results are never stratified by onboarding month, by academic breaks for the campus-heavy BDG2, or by heating/cooling transitions. BDG2 uses observed temperature (Limitation 3), and no test perturbs it. Calibration scores always come from the year immediately before the target.
issues.action: Stratify existing results by onboarding month or season. Add the experiments listed.
issues.experiment: (a) Calibration onboarding restricted to one season (e.g. winter) with targets onboarded in another (summer). (b) Temperature inputs perturbed with realistic day-ahead forecast errors (e.g. N(0, 1.5-3 K) with autocorrelation). (c) Windows spanning holidays or semester breaks, evaluated separately.

issues.title: Text on robustness overstates or misattributes results
issues.evidence: Sec 5.5 says 'HSC-CQR leaves 1.7% under-covered because the building's own, noisy scores enter the mixture' but omits that Self-CQR is lower (0.1%). The Conclusion says the method 'remained beneficial ... under abrupt level changes' while ACI-CQR and QShrink were not tested against it statistically. Table 6 shows the weak-forecaster MLP-QR as '–' without explanation in the text.
issues.action: Report the best method per condition and qualify the claims accordingly.

issues.title: Target population selected on target-period data quality, using a post-hoc filter triggered by target-period diagnostics
issues.evidence: datasets.py:99-106 (BDG2) and 141-147 (UCI) keep a building only if <=5% of hours are missing AND mean >=1 kWh/h in EVERY year, including the evaluation years (2017 / 2014). CHANGELOG.md:6-9 says the >=24 h stuck-run rule was added after smoke-test diagnostics on Lamb-site meters 'flat-lined ... in 2017' (the target year), which cut BDG2 from 984 to 842 buildings. The Lamb site is gone (10 sites remain; BDG2 has 19 sites and about 1.5k electricity meters). PREREGISTRATION.md has no data-cleaning or quality-filter section, yet Sec. 4.1 says the rules were 'fixed before the main experiments' and the abstract calls the protocol 'pre-registered'. Because of the year-level filter, the 80% valid-window rule hardly ever binds: 86.8% of BDG2 target windows and 99.6% of UCI windows have all 1344 h valid (raw_results.csv.gz). The result is that newly metered buildings with outages, stuck meters or commissioning problems in the target year are excluded by look-ahead. This is the failure mode that Limitation 4 says is only 'approximated'.
issues.action: Add a per-site attrition table (raw meters, then after each rule, then final). Apply year-level filters only to training and calibration buildings and periods. Select target buildings with an operational, non-look-ahead rule (e.g. only the 80% window rule, or none). Correct the pre-registration claim and state openly that the stuck-meter rule was data-driven.
issues.experiment: Re-run the main BDG2 and UCI comparison (Tables 2-4) on the enlarged target set chosen without target-year filtering. Report the under-covered share and MACD next to the current numbers.

issues.title: Imputation fills parts of long gaps and leaks future readings into features and ground truth
issues.evidence: _clean_hourly (datasets.py:64) calls out.interpolate(limit=6, limit_area='inside'). In pandas, limit=6 fills the FIRST 6 NaNs of any longer gap rather than leaving it untouched. Verified: [1, NaN x10, 12] becomes [1,2,3,4,5,6,7,NaN,...,12]. So the first 6 h of every masked >=24 h stuck run, and of every longer outage, are linearly interpolated toward a reading taken a day or more later. This contradicts Sec. 4.1 ('gaps of at most 6 h are linearly interpolated'). Cleaning runs on the whole series before the cube is built, so history features for day t (lag1d, prev_max/min, the scale s) can hold values interpolated from day-t or later readings. The unit test test_features_use_only_history_window (tests/test_core.py:18) uses gap-free toy data, so it cannot catch this. Imputed hours also count as valid ground truth: interval_metrics uses only ~isnan. Under-coverage is higher in windows with missing hours (CQR 22.8% vs 18.0%), so imputation choices affect the headline numbers.
issues.action: Interpolate only gaps of 6 h or less, using an explicit run-length mask. For features, use only causal (forward-looking-only) imputation, or impute within the history window. Flag imputed hours and leave them out of coverage and IS. Add a unit test with gaps that cross the history/target boundary. Report the share of imputed target hours.
issues.experiment: Re-run the main protocol with the corrected cleaning. At minimum, re-evaluate the existing predictions with imputed hours masked.

issues.title: Headline under-coverage is concentrated in two sites; there is no site-level reporting
issues.evidence: raw_results.csv.gz, random protocol, BDG2, alpha=0.1: Rat contributes 218 of 713 unique target buildings, and Rat plus Wolf make up 35% of building x seed units. They account for 58% of CQR's under-covered units (53% for HSC-CQR). Wolf: CQR 60.0% / HSC-CQR 13.3% under-covered, median CV(RMSE) 0.30 vs 0.10-0.16 elsewhere. Without Rat and Wolf, CQR under-coverage falls from 18.7% to 12.0% and HSC-CQR from 3.4% to 2.5%. Because building-weighted pooling is used, 18.7% largely describes Rat and Wolf rather than 'new buildings' in general.
issues.action: Report per-site under-coverage and MACD for all methods, plus site-weighted (macro) averages next to the building-weighted ones. Check whether Wolf's problems come from data (cleaning artefacts, meter type) rather than behaviour. Soften the abstract's generalisation accordingly.
issues.experiment: No new training needed; recompute the tables from raw_results.

issues.title: Calibration scores are temporally in-sample for the forecaster while targets are out-of-period, which confounds heterogeneity with temporal shift
issues.evidence: pipeline.py: train_models samples training-building rows from the entire training period, and calibration buildings are onboarded in the SAME period (Sec. 4.2; onboard_dates called with the training period). In the random protocol, calibration buildings share sites, weather and campus calendars (holidays, closures) with training buildings at the same dates, so their CQR scores come from conditions the model was fitted on. Target scores come from 2017. Methods that use the target's own 2017 scores (HSC, Self, QShrink) can correct this shift; pooled CQR cannot. A deployed system would have recent out-of-sample scores from previously onboarded buildings. The mean coverage of pooled CQR (0.891) suggests a modest effect, but its per-building contribution is unknown. run_info.json stores only LOBO objectives, not calibration-period coverage.
issues.action: Report CQR coverage on calibration buildings under LOBO next to target coverage. Add a protocol variant where calibration buildings are onboarded in the target year, before each target's onboarding date (or in a held-out early-2017 block not used for training).
issues.experiment: One extra run of the main BDG2 comparison (5 seeds) with out-of-period calibration windows.

issues.title: Weather: oracle temperature and unverified timestamp alignment
issues.evidence: features.py:118-127 uses observed temperature for the target day (temp, temp_daymean). Limitation 3 says this 'favours point accuracy for all methods equally'. This is unsupported: oracle weather lowers the residuals of weather-sensitive buildings specifically and so compresses the between-building score heterogeneity being studied. The meta 'timezone' column is loaded (datasets.py:118) but never used anywhere in src/ (grep). Site weather is reindexed directly onto meter timestamps (datasets.py:108-114). For the GEPIII/BDG2 weather files, a UTC vs local-time offset has been widely reported, so the temperature-hour alignment has to be checked.
issues.action: Check meter/weather alignment (lag cross-correlation of load vs temperature per site) and fix any offset. Replace the 'equally' claim with evidence: report the main-table ranking on the existing BDG2->BDG2 no-weather runs, or use forecast-like temperature (persistence or noise-perturbed).
issues.experiment: Lag-alignment check (cheap). Optionally re-run BDG2 main with temperature forecasts perturbed by a realistic day-ahead error.

issues.title: No duplicate or nested-meter check; UCI DST artefacts not handled
issues.evidence: Neither datasets.py nor pipeline.py checks for near-duplicate series or main/sub-meter nesting across training, calibration and target sets. In the random protocol, co-located buildings regularly fall into different sets. load_uci (datasets.py:136-139) only shifts by 15 min. The known UCI DST convention (a zero hour in March, two hours merged in October) is left in place, so the March-2014 zero hour is a valid 'truth' inside target windows and produces spurious misses.
issues.action: Report pairwise correlation (e.g. r>0.99 on training-year series) and identical-series checks, and drop or group duplicates before splitting. Mask the DST hours in UCI.
issues.experiment: None beyond a data check; re-run only if duplicates are found.

result.summary:
This is the dataset and leakage review, cycle 1. The features themselves respect the history window (features.py and descriptor use only days t-min(h,28)..t-1). Splits are building-disjoint, and hyperparameters are tuned only on calibration buildings. Both licences (CC-BY-4.0) are stated correctly. However, the data pipeline weakens the evaluation in four ways.

(1) Target buildings are selected by look-ahead filtering. The <=5%-missing and >=1 kWh/h rules are applied to the target year, and the stuck-meter rule was added after seeing target-year (2017) artefacts at the Lamb site (984 to 842 buildings). It is not in PREREGISTRATION.md, so newly metered buildings with real-world data problems are systematically excluded and the 80% window rule is almost moot.

(2) pandas interpolate(limit=6) fills the first 6 h of every longer gap, including masked stuck runs. It uses later readings to do so, which leaks future information into history features and into imputed ground truth. The manuscript's description of the rule is also wrong, and the unit tests cannot detect this.

(3) The headline under-coverage figures are dominated by two sites: Rat and Wolf make up 35% of units but 58% of CQR's under-covered units. Without them, CQR falls from 18.7% to 12.0% and HSC-CQR from 3.4% to 2.5%. No per-site reporting is given.

(4) Calibration scores come from the forecaster's training period while targets come from the following year. This mixes temporal shift into the 'per-building heterogeneity' story and favours methods that use the target's own scores.

Weather is oracle, and the meter/weather timezone alignment is unverified (the timezone column is never used). There are no duplicate-meter checks.

The main conclusion (shrinkage beats pooled CQR) will probably survive, but the reported magnitudes and the 'pre-registered' claim need fixing. Required: corrected cleaning, re-running with targets not selected by look-ahead, an out-of-period calibration variant, and site-level tables.

Computational efficiency review, cycle 1. The calibration layer is clearly cheap. In the recommended simple variant it is a single 4000-point pooled CDF plus each building's running counts, and the operation is O(NG) per building-day, so I don't doubt that it can be deployed. However, the cost evidence in Table 8, Section 5.7, Section 6.3 and the abstract is measured for the wrong variant, partly contaminated, and described inaccurately. (1) The reported 0.437 ms and 36.7 s are timings of the absolute-score HSC with a kNN prior (K=25 on BDG2), not of HSC-CQR or of the one-parameter 'HSC-CQR simple' layer that the abstract attributes them to (src/training/pipeline.py:311-322). HSC-CQR tuning is never timed. (2) The UCI seed-1 training time is a known OpenMP-oversubscription stall: LightGBM 1316.7 s against 26.8-51.6 s for the other seeds. It is still averaged into Table 8, which inflates the UCI training times about 6x. Calibration timings come from four concurrent single-threaded workers, measured once with time.time(), while the caption says '4-core CPU'. (3) 'Per building-day' is batch throughput, not update latency, and the inference figure covers only one of the three LightGBM models CQR needs. (4) The 'negligible' and 'portfolio-scale' claims are not quantified; the full kNN variant has quadratic and K×NG memory terms. None of this changes the scientific conclusions, but the numbers in the abstract and Table 8 must be re-measured on the right variant in a clean, repeated benchmark before acceptance.

issues.title: The headline cost (0.437 ms, 36.7 s) is measured for a different variant than the one the abstract and Section 6.3 recommend
issues.evidence: pipeline.py:311-322 times tune_hsc(Sc, ...) and hsc_quantiles(cc_t, binc, nbrs_by_stage(zt, zc, best['K']), ...) on the absolute-residual scores with the kNN prior. run_info.json main_BDG2_s0_a0.1 gives hsc_K=25, hsc_kappa=168. Neither the HSC-CQR tuning (pipeline.py:338, grid over K∈{10,25,50,100,all} × 9 κ) nor the HSC-CQR simple tuning/apply (pipeline.py:355-362) is timed. Yet the abstract says 'a one-parameter layer whose pseudo-count ... costs 0.437 ms per building-day'. hsc_store_MB (pipeline.py:322) is likewise for the absolute-score per-bin store.
issues.action: Time HSC-CQR and HSC-CQR simple separately (tuning and apply) and report both in Table 8. Correct the abstract and Section 5.7 to quote the variant actually recommended. Also reword the abstract so the cost belongs to the layer, not to 'the pseudo-count'.
issues.experiment: Timing-only rerun on the cached predictions; no model retraining needed.

issues.title: Timing data contaminated by a documented oversubscription stall and by concurrent workers; single uncontrolled measurement
issues.evidence: T_efficiency.md main_UCI_s1: lgb_train_s 1316.66 and mlp_train_s 929.31, against 26.8-51.6 s and 64.2-70.8 s for the other UCI seeds. CHANGELOG.md:24-25 records 'OpenMP thread oversubscription ... no progress for 33 min'. Table 8 still reports the UCI mean, 298 s / 239 s (median ≈46 s / 67 s). This makes UCI look about 3x costlier than BDG2 with fewer rows (1.0 M vs 1.32 M). Calibration was run as four simultaneous single-threaded workers (scripts/calibration_pass.sh:6-17), but Table 8 says '4-core CPU'. Each value is one time.time() call. The spread is HSC apply 0.175-0.639 ms (BDG2) and 0.068-0.467 ms (UCI), and LightGBM inference 0.046-1.319 ms, a factor of up to 28. BDG2 inference (0.668 ms) is 6x UCI's (0.106 ms) for nearly the same feature set, which points to contention, not workload.
issues.action: Run a dedicated benchmark in isolation: no concurrent jobs, fixed thread counts, warm-up, ≥10 repetitions, CPU model reported. Report the median and IQR, not a 5-seed mean. Exclude or rerun UCI seed 1, and state the thread configuration in the caption.
issues.experiment: Isolated micro-benchmark of training (one seed), inference and calibration per dataset.

issues.title: 'Per building-day' is amortised batch throughput and understates end-to-end serving cost
issues.evidence: pipeline.py:320-321 divides one vectorised call over all targets × 56 stages by (St.shape[0]*NH). That is not the latency of the operational daily update for one building, which in the code also involves neighbour search on standardised descriptors. LightGBM inference (pipeline.py:162-163) times only models['lgb'].predict. The CQR path also needs lgb_lo and lgb_hi (lines 164-165), so the inference cost for HSC-CQR is about 3x the reported 0.668 ms. Feature construction (fe.build) is not timed at all.
issues.action: Report both single-building incremental-update latency and batch throughput. Time all three LightGBM predictions plus feature construction, and give an end-to-end per-building-day cost for the CQR pipeline.
issues.experiment: Timing-only.

issues.title: Scalability and 'negligible' claims not supported for portfolio scale
issues.evidence: Section 5.7 calls tuning (36.7 s) 'negligible next to' 106 s of LightGBM training, but that is 35% of it. calibration_total_s (285-339 s on BDG2) exceeds train_total_s (189-257 s). In the full variant, neighbours() builds an (nt, M, d) array (calibration.py:136), and prior_cdf materialises cal_cdf_k[nbr] as (nt, K, NG) float32 (calibration.py:160): 170×100×4000×4 B ≈ 272 MB per stage call during LOBO tuning, and ≈3.2 GB at M=2000. Tuning cost grows as O(M·K·NG·|κ|·56) plus O(M²·d). Section 6.3 claims 'compatible with portfolio-scale deployment', but the largest tested configuration has ~170 calibration and ~253 target buildings.
issues.action: Add a complexity table (time and memory per target-day, per tuning run, for full and simple variants) and a scaling curve over the calibration-pool size M and number of targets. Make clear that the simple variant avoids the K×NG and M² terms. Tone down 'negligible' or quantify it as a fraction of the total pipeline.
issues.experiment: Synthetic scaling test: resample calibration/target buildings to M = 170, 1k, 5k, 10k, timing tuning and apply for both variants.

issues.title: Memory accounting is incomplete and not for the deployed variant
issues.evidence: hsc_store_MB = binc.astype(float32).nbytes + zc.nbytes (pipeline.py:322), which is per-calibration-building × 7 stage bins × 4000 points: 19.79 MB / ~170 buildings ≈ 0.116 MB per building. Per-target state is excluded. In the code, cum_counts holds (nt, 56, 4000) int16 ≈ 0.45 MB per target (calibration.py:48), whereas deployment needs only running counts (16 kB). The simple variant needs a single pooled 4000-vector.
issues.action: Report memory for the recommended variant: pooled store plus per-building state. Extrapolate to 10^4-10^5 buildings, and note that int16/int32 counts suffice.
issues.experiment: None (analytic).

issues.title: No cost comparison with the competing strategies, and no grid-resolution trade-off
issues.evidence: QShrink-CQR is within 0.004 MACD of HSC-CQR on BDG2 (Table 4: −0.0047 CD; IS p=0.688). ACI-CQR and Self-CQR have the same order of cost. Table 8 gives cost only for HSC, so a reader cannot tell whether cost discriminates between methods. The 4000-point asinh grid with upward rounding (Section 3.4) is applied to all methods, but its accuracy/cost trade-off, and how often the quantile hits the 500·s cap, are not reported.
issues.action: Add per-method calibration time (tuning and apply), and state explicitly that all adaptive strategies are sub-millisecond, so cost does not discriminate. Report how sensitive the results are to grid size (e.g. 1000/4000/16000 points), or an exact sorted-score check on one seed, plus the frequency of capped radii.
issues.experiment: Optional one-seed grid-resolution check.

result.summary: Literature and citation review, cycle 1. I could not use Crossref, arXiv or Zenodo directly because the session's network proxy blocks api.crossref.org, arxiv.org and zenodo.org; those hosts would need to be allowed to repeat the checks. Instead I checked 12 references with WebSearch and against the repository's own verification records (literature/references_verified*.json). Seven matched the manuscript on authors, year, venue and pages, or on arXiv ID: Hong 2023 (NAAJ 27(4):675-688), Rafe & Das (arXiv 2605.05562), Mallick et al. (arXiv 2608.15500), Bühlmann (as a missing reference), Suresh 2025, Moradi 2025 and Ristovska 2026. Hao 2026 [14] and Shi 2026 [35] have Crossref or interactive records in the repo, but I could not find them independently on the web. The reference list is mostly accurate and nothing looks fabricated. The problems are citation support and coverage, not invented references: (i) the 'classical credibility form' is credited to a 2023 conformal paper instead of Bühlmann's credibility theory; (ii) one reference whose abstract the authors say they could not read ([35]) supports a substantive general claim; (iii) the closest prior art ([26]-[29]) is entirely unrefereed preprints or a software record, while refereed foundations are missing; (iv) several directly competing method families are neither cited nor discussed: localized conformal prediction, conformal PID control/SPCI, ensemble CQR for energy, quantile forecasting of individual smart-meter loads, and DR/M&V baseline literature. None of this affects the empirical results, but the novelty positioning and the AAE-facing motivation need tightening.

issues.title: Credibility weight n/(n+n0) credited to the wrong source
issues.evidence: Sec. 2.3 and Eq. (5): 'the classical credibility form [52]'. [52] is Hong L. 'Conformal prediction credibility intervals', NAAJ 2023;27:675-88 (confirmed via WebSearch/IDEAS). That paper wraps a conformal interval around a credibility estimator. It is not the origin of the classical credibility weight, which comes from Bühlmann, 'Experience rating and credibility', ASTIN Bull. 1967;4(3):199-207, and the empirical-Bayes tradition (Robbins; Efron & Morris). The manuscript calls the layer 'empirical Bayes' (keywords) but cites no empirical-Bayes source.
issues.action: Cite Bühlmann (1967), and optionally Bühlmann & Gisler (2005) and Efron & Morris (1973/1975), for the credibility/empirical-Bayes form. Keep Hong (2023) only as an example of combining conformal prediction with credibility estimators.

issues.title: Directly competing method families are missing
issues.evidence: Neither the manuscript sections nor literature/*.md mention localized conformal prediction (Guan, Biometrika 2023), which is the natural reference and competitor for the kNN 'similarity-localised prior' (Eq. 4). Also missing: conformal PID control (Angelopoulos, Candès & Tibshirani, NeurIPS 2023) and SPCI (Xu & Xie, ICML 2023), the current successors of ACI, which is criticised in Sec. 6.1 as 'slow from a poor starting point'; ensemble CQR for energy time series (Jensen, Bianchi & Anfinsen, IEEE TNNLS 2022); and quantile forecasting of individual smart-meter loads (Taieb et al., IEEE TSG 2016). A grep of manuscript/sections and literature/*.md for 'localized conformal|Guan|PID|SPCI|Taieb|EnCQR|Jensen' returns nothing.
issues.action: Add these to Sec. 2.3 and 2.1. State explicitly why ACI is the representative online method and how the kNN prior relates to localized CP. Also add PID/quantile-tracking to Limitation 7 as an untested online competitor.
issues.experiment: Optional: a conformal-PID (quantile-tracking) variant on CQR scores in the main BDG2/UCI protocol, using the existing LOBO tuning of its step size. This would directly answer the 'ACI is slow' argument.

issues.title: A claim rests on a reference the authors could not read
issues.evidence: literature/verify_refs_new.py:42 notes for 10.1016/j.epsr.2026.113412 (Shi, Shen & Lyu): 'abstract not accessible -> cited only for what its title states'. Yet Sec. 2.1 groups [35] with [18,19] and then claims 'These works assess reliability with *pooled* metrics over a site, a system or a test period, typically for systems with long histories'. The authors cannot back that claim for [35]. A 'local' online CP method may well evaluate locally conditional coverage.
issues.action: Get and read [35] and check the claim, or remove [35] from the sentence that asserts what these works evaluate.

issues.title: Closest prior art is all unrefereed
issues.evidence: The novelty paragraph (Sec. 2.3, 'not new as a mechanism') rests on [26] Shahid 2026 (arXiv, workshop submission), [27] Rafe & Das 2026 (arXiv), [28] Zhang et al. 2024 (arXiv), [29] Jeon 2026 (a Zenodo software record, not a paper) and [25] GHCP (arXiv, Aug 2026). In total, 11 of the 62 references are preprints or software. Two of them are the basis for named baselines (GHCP-CQR, QShrink-CQR), and the descriptions of those baselines cannot be checked against peer-reviewed text. WebSearch also shows that [27]'s regularised Mondrian uses a fixed λ=50 (w=n_g/(n_g+50)), whereas QShrink-CQR selects λ by LOBO. That difference is not stated.
issues.action: Add refereed anchors (Bühlmann; Guan 2023; Dunn et al. [23] is already cited). Mark [29] as a software record in the text. Note that QShrink-CQR differs from [27] in tuning λ (the original uses a fixed λ=50). Update preprint citations to published versions where they exist.

issues.title: AAE-facing application claims have no citations
issues.evidence: The Intro and Sec. 6.3 claim that DR baselines, M&V, settlements and alarms need per-building intervals and that under-covered buildings mean 'systematically under-protected baselines ... settlements'. The only domain citation is [1] (a flexibility review). There is no reference on DR baseline or M&V uncertainty (e.g., Granderson et al., Appl Energy 2016, on automated M&V accuracy; ASHRAE Guideline 14 [59] is cited only for CV(RMSE)). Sec. 6.3 also says the layer is compatible 'with pretrained forecasting models', which is untested and uncited.
issues.action: Add 2-3 references on DR baseline/M&V uncertainty requirements and link the under-coverage metric to them. Soften or cite the pretrained-model compatibility claim (BuildingsBench [13]; Chronos/TimesFM).

issues.title: Reference metadata gaps
issues.evidence: [44] Lin et al. (TMLR 2022) gives an arXiv DOI instead of the OpenReview/TMLR record. [61] Holm 1979 has no DOI or stable URL (JSTOR 4615733). In literature/references_verified_new.json, the UCI dataset DOI 10.24432/C58C86 is recorded ok=false. manuscript/references.py:3 cites 'literature/citation_audit.md', which does not exist in literature/. 'paszke2019' is in REFS but never cited.
issues.action: Fix the [44] and [61] identifiers. Re-run the UCI DOI check via DataCite. Add the missing citation_audit.md or remove the pointer. Prune unused entries.

issues.title: Reference [14] could not be confirmed independently
issues.evidence: Hao, Yang & Ji, Appl Sci 2026;16:7984 is cited twice as the key motivating evidence that split-conformal under-covers unseen buildings. An exact-title WebSearch found nothing. Only the repository's Crossref record (references_verified_new.json entry 10) supports it, and the matrix does not record that the full text was read.
issues.action: Confirm that the full text supports 'under-covers on average ... recommends recalibration', and add a page or section pointer in the citation audit.

result.summary:
AE assessment, cycle 1. The topic fits Advances in Applied Energy: reliable per-building day-ahead intervals while new buildings are being onboarded. The experiments go deeper than the journal norm (literature/aae_benchmark.md: two datasets, 1,157 units, 5 seeds, leave-site-out, cross-country transfer, stress tests, paired statistics). The numbers I checked match the result files. Format checks pass: abstract 215 words, highlights all under 85 characters, competing-interest and generative-AI declarations present.

The desk-rejection risk is still high, for four reasons. (1) The paper compares known mechanisms, and the authors themselves say the pseudo-count mixture is not new. (2) The one thing that sets it apart from [29], choosing kappa by leave-one-building-out, gives less reliable coverage than a fixed kappa = 168 h. (3) The paper never puts a number on the operational energy payoff that AAE papers usually show. (4) The claim that everything was pre-registered contradicts the CHANGELOG, and the headline method is the full variant that the paper's own conclusion calls unnecessary.

Claims of being "most reliable" over quantile shrinkage (QShrink-CQR) and self-only calibration (Self-CQR) are overstated in leave-site-out and in several stress tests. ACI interval-score means are distorted by a radius-cap artefact. The manuscript is about twice the journal's length (29-page PDF). These problems can be fixed without new core experiments, apart from adding a downstream operational evaluation.

issues.title: Thin novelty for AAE: the recommended method is a known mechanism, its distinguishing feature (LOBO-tuned kappa) is worse than a fixed kappa, and no operational energy value is shown
issues.evidence: Sec. 2.3 says the pseudo-count mixture 'is therefore not new as a mechanism'. The stated difference from [29] is selecting kappa by leave-one-building-out (LOBO) instead of fixing it. On BDG2, though, HSC-CQR fixed-κ (κ=168 h) beats the tuned HSC-CQR on reliability: MACD 0.015 vs 0.018 and under-covered share 1.9% vs 3.4% (Table 5). The paired test also favours fixed-κ on coverage deviation: Table 4 row 'HSC-CQR fixed-κ CD', mean diff +0.0026, CI [+0.0015, +0.0036], r_rb = -0.45. The benchmark (literature/aae_benchmark.md, conclusions 1 and 6) says AAE papers quantify an operational payoff. Here every result is a statistical metric (MACD, IS); demand-response baselines, flexibility bids and M&V are named in the Introduction but never evaluated.
issues.action: Recast the contribution as a benchmark plus a deployment rule, and state openly that the LOBO interval-score objective trades away reliability. Add an energy-application evaluation, e.g. demand-response baseline settlement error or penalty exposure, or flexibility-bid shortfall probability or cost, under pooled CQR vs shrinkage, so the 18.7% to 3.4% gain gets an operational meaning. Alternatively, tune kappa on a reliability-aware objective chosen in advance.
issues.experiment: Downstream case study on the existing per-building intervals: simulate DR baseline or flexibility-bid settlement for the BDG2 target buildings and report the cost or violation rate by method. No retraining needed.

issues.title: Pre-registration claims do not match the record; the outcome of the pre-registered hypothesis is not reported
issues.evidence: manuscript/sections/05_setup.md:55 says 'All settings were fixed in a pre-registration file before any full experiment was run'; the abstract and contribution 1 call the protocol 'pre-registered'. The CHANGELOG entry of 2026-11-16 adds GHCP-CQR, QShrink-CQR, TQA-B-CQR, HSC(-CQR) simple, fixed-κ and MLP-CQR, extends the ACI grid, and replaces ablations. This came after the self-audit row 'First full-run look (seed 0 BDG2): kNN localisation and stage matching show ~no benefit'. The pre-registered H0 (PREREGISTRATION.md) concerns stage-matched, kNN-localised HSC improving MACD and IS. Abs-score HSC has IS 0.642 vs 0.639 for stage-matched pooled conformal (SCP-stage), and its MACD (0.029) is worse than self-only calibration Self-CP (0.026) (Table 2), so H0 fails on IS. PREREGISTRATION.md lists 'HSC on CQR scores (variant)' among the baselines, yet the CHANGELOG says the 'pre-registered primary comparison remains HSC-CQR'.
issues.action: Add a table of deviations from the pre-registration (added baselines and variants, ACI grid, removed ablations, change of primary method) with dates and reasons. State plainly that the pre-registered H0 was not supported for abs-score HSC and its refinements. Mark which comparisons are confirmatory and which exploratory. Replace 'all settings were fixed…' with an accurate sentence, and qualify 'pre-registered' in the abstract.
issues.experiment: None

issues.title: The headline method is the full variant the paper calls unnecessary
issues.evidence: Abstract, highlights, Table 4, Sec. 5.2 and the Conclusion all report full HSC-CQR (kNN prior plus stage matching): under-covered 3.4%, P10 0.864. Yet the paper concludes the refinements 'add nothing'. HSC-CQR simple is better on every reliability metric: 2.9%, P10 0.869, MACD 0.017 (Table 2). The full variant's first-week coverage, 0.885, is below pooled CQR (0.892) and simple (0.895). Fig. 1 (figures/Fig1_method.png) still draws the stage-matched kNN prior as the method. The recommended one-parameter layer has no paired tests against the baselines.
issues.action: Make HSC-CQR simple (or fixed-κ) the primary method in the abstract, highlights, Table 4 and the Conclusion, and keep the full variant as an ablation. Redraw Fig. 1 around the one-parameter layer.
issues.experiment: Re-run the statistics script (Wilcoxon + Holm + cluster bootstrap) for HSC-CQR simple against all baselines on the existing raw_results. No new runs.

issues.title: 'Most reliable strategy' is overstated compared with quantile shrinkage and self-only calibration
issues.evidence: BDG2 random protocol: QShrink-CQR MACD 0.022 ± 0.004 vs 0.018 ± 0.001; interval score indistinguishable (p = 0.688, Table 4). Leave-site-out under-covered share: QShrink-CQR 4.2% vs HSC-CQR 5.3% (Table 7). Table 6 stress tests: calibration pool 10%, QShrink 0.019/6 vs HSC-CQR 0.020/8; missing 20%, 3 vs 4; noise 15%, Self-CQR 0.010/0 vs 0.018/2. UCI→BDG2: Self-CQR 6.9% vs 8.7%. Sec. 6.4(8) concedes the differences among the best strategies are partly within per-building sampling noise.
issues.action: Reword the abstract, highlights (bullet 4) and Conclusion to say that shrinkage strategies, whether on the score distribution or on quantiles, are the most reliable family, with a small and consistent paired advantage for distribution mixing on the random protocol. Say explicitly where QShrink-CQR or Self-CQR match or beat it.
issues.experiment: None

issues.title: ACI interval-score means are dominated by the 500·s radius cap
issues.evidence: In results/raw_results.csv.gz, per-building rel_IS for ACI-CQR reaches 551 (BDG2) and 337 (UCI); for HSC-CQR the maxima are 17.6 and 8.7. This follows the convention of setting the radius to the largest grid value (500·s) when α_h ≤ 0 (Sec. 4.3). The result is Table 4 mean differences of -0.1718 (BDG2) and -1.9143 (UCI), the latter with CI [-4.5953, -0.1544], which describe the artefact rather than typical behaviour.
issues.action: For IS, report median paired differences or Hodges–Lehmann estimates with CIs. Report how often each method hits the cap. Add a sensitivity row for ACI with α_h clipped to [ε, 1-ε].
issues.experiment: Recompute ACI-CQR with clipped α_h on stored scores (calibration-only pass).

issues.title: Manuscript about twice AAE's length; tables duplicate each other
issues.evidence: manuscript/Final_Manuscript.pdf has 29 pages. The body is about 8,250 words excluding tables, plus 8 tables and 11 figures. Table 7 has 45 rows, and its 'BDG2 random' and 'UCI random' blocks repeat Tables 2/3. Table 5 repeats rows of Table 2. Table 8 and Fig. 11 add little. The journal target is about 10-15 printed pages.
issues.action: Move Table 6, Table 8, Fig. 9 and Fig. 11, and the abs-score variants, to the SI. Drop the duplicated random-protocol rows from Table 7. Cut Tables 2/3 to the CQR-score family plus key baselines. Aim for about 6,000 words.
issues.experiment: None

issues.title: Figure files numbered differently from the figures; the most reliable variant is missing from Fig. 4
issues.evidence: Fig. 3 is figures/Fig4_coverage_cdf.png, Fig. 4 is Fig5_tradeoff.png and Fig. 5 is Fig3_stage_curves.png. Fig. 4 (trade-off) shows HSC-CQR simple and full but omits HSC-CQR fixed-κ, which has the lowest MACD (Table 5).
issues.action: Rename the files so they match the figure order for the Elsevier submission system, and add fixed-κ to Fig. 4.
issues.experiment: None

issues.title: Error-analysis tests treat building × seed units as independent
issues.evidence: Sec. 5.8 runs Mann–Whitney tests on 43 of 1,265 building × seed units (BDG2) and 3 of 475 (UCI). The same building appears as a target in several seeds, so the units are not independent. With only 3 UCI units, a p < 0.001 claim is fragile.
issues.action: Collapse to one unit per building (seed-averaged coverage) before testing, or use a cluster permutation test. Report UCI descriptively.
issues.experiment: None (re-analysis of existing results)

issues.title: Declarations and data availability incomplete for submission
issues.evidence: CRediT, affiliations and acknowledgements are placeholders. The code statement says '[repository URL to be inserted upon acceptance]'. The AI-use statement contains an author-instruction note.
issues.action: Complete all declarations. Deposit code and results in a persistent archive (e.g. Zenodo DOI) before submission and cite it in the data availability statement.
